summary: 60 Seconds to Mars is a free, browser-based survival game for kids aged 7–12 in which a crew of junior cadets must keep the Ares-IV outpost in Jezero Crater alive through a real solar storm. Players first win supplies in a 60-second space trivia, then manage five connected systems (oxygen, power, food, radiation shielding and crew health) over 5 or 10 Martian Sols. Every decision has a real engineering cost: no choice is free, which turns NASA's mission trade-offs into something kids can feel and understand. The game is grounded in live NASA open data. NASA DONKI drives the solar flares and radiation risk. NASA OSDR/GeneLab informs life support and greenhouse dilemmas. Real Perseverance photos from the NASA Image and Video Library arrive as transmissions from Earth, and communication delay is modelled with the real Earth–Mars light time. Gemini AI acts as a child-safe Game Master, so every playthrough is different. An onboard assistant reads everything aloud, so children who are still learning to read can play on their own. We want kids to walk away understanding why surviving on Mars is a matter of decisions, not luck.
details:
What it is

60 Seconds to Mars is an educational web game (no download, no account) for children aged 7–12, available in Spanish and English and playable on desktop and mobile. It is the year 2038. A real solar flare detected by NASA DONKI cuts off the adult astronauts' rover, and three junior cadets (Leo, Vega and the player) must keep the Ares-IV base alive with the help of A.R.I.A., the onboard AI.

How it works

  1. Mission profile: Choose between “Explorer mode” (ages 7+, 2 answer options, 5-Sol mission) and “Commander mode” (up to age 12, 4 answer options, 10-Sol mission with tighter reserves). 
  2. Phase 1 – 60-second trivia: 45 questions about life support, power, food, radiation and health, with progressive difficulty. Each right answer sends a real piece of equipment to the base (30 items, each with a NASA fact and source). Failing a whole system causes an initial breakdown, so knowledge has consequences.
  3. Phase 2 – Survival (5/10 Sols): Players switch machines on and off and balance five connected bars: every machine consumes power, radiation erodes shielding, and low shielding, oxygen or food hurts crew health. Each Sol brings a daily dilemma generated by Gemini (with an offline fallback). A validator guarantees that every option carries a real cost, so there is never a "free" safe choice.
  4. Communication delay: Ordering supplies from Houston via the Deep Space Network costs power today and arrives two Sols later, based on the real Earth–Mars distance and light delay. Kids learn to plan ahead.
  5. Repairs: Breakdowns are fixed through quick mini-games (cables, solar panel radio tuning, sealing leaks with Kapton tape, orbital debris). Each one shows a real data point.
  6. Rescue: If the crew survives every Sol, players drive a 3D rover across Jezero Crater to the Earth Return Rocket, dodging rocks within 60 seconds. Keyboard and touch controls are supported.
  7. Debriefing: An engineering report explains the best decision, what to improve and science lessons. If a bar reaches zero there is no dramatic "game over", only a medical evacuation to orbit plus an analysis of what went wrong and how to improve, so that kids keep being motivated to keep playing.

Benefits

  • Tangible trade-offs: Makes real mission trade-offs tangible: saving power today can cost oxygen tomorrow.
  • Real, traceable science: An in-game "NASA Open Data Used" panel shows each dataset, whether it is LIVE or a CURATED ARCHIVE in that session, and which mechanic it drives. We never present archived data as live.
  • Replayability: Real solar activity, AI-generated events, random breakdowns and a weighted supply capsule make each mission different.
  • Accessibility: Every screen is read aloud, there is a kid-friendly glossary (Sol, radiation/CME, solar flare, microgravity), plain language, two difficulty levels and two languages.
  • Personalisation: An optional Cadet Badge takes a webcam photo of the player, which is processed 100% in the browser and never uploaded, and puts them in the crew, just as with their name, and their role.

Our Goal

Close the gap the challenge describes: space content for kids is either too abstract or too technical. We want children to experience the decision-making logic behind a real mission, and teachers to have a free tool they can open in class straight from a link.

Tools and Technologies

  • Front end: TypeScript, React 19, Vite, Tailwind CSS 4, Framer Motion, Zustand, Three.js (procedural 3D rover scene), lucide-react.
  • Audio and voice: Web Speech API (voice and voice commands) and Web Audio API (all sound effects are synthesised, no audio files).
  • AI: Google Gemini (@google/genai), behind a server-side proxy (Cloudflare Pages Functions) that hides the API key, restricts requests to the game's origin and rate-limits them.
  • Hosting: Cloudflare Pages. Source on GitHub.
  • Version Control & Team Workflow (Git Flow): The repository is hosted inside a dedicated GitHub Organization managed by two repository owners (NASA-SpaceApps-2026). To keep the codebase stable during rapid hackathon development, we enforce a strict branch protection and Git Flow model:
    • Protected Branches: Direct pushes to develop and main are completely blocked.
    • Feature Branches & Pull Requests: All development happens in isolated feature branches (e.g., feature/my-change). Changes are integrated into develop via Pull Requests (PRs), and releases are promoted from develop to main via PRs.
    • Automated Status Checks & Reviews: Every Pull Request triggers automated CI checks (TypeScript compilation and production build verification via npm run build in GitHub Actions) and requires peer/owner review before merging, ensuring broken code never reaches production.
